summary: Sets guidelines for developers on human rights considerations in protocols and architectures, in the spirit of the privacy considerations in RFC 6973. It updates RFC 8280 and comes from the IRTF Human Rights Protocol Considerations Research Group.

eli5.summary: This is a checklist for people who design the Internet to think about how their choices affect people's freedoms.

subtitle: A questionnaire for protocol designers on how their technical choices can help or harm human rights on the Internet.

tldr.problem: Protocol and architecture decisions can affect rights such as freedom of expression, association and privacy, but engineers have had little structured guidance for thinking about this.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC offers methods for human rights reviews of Internet-Drafts and a questionnaire of 21 considerations, each with questions, an explanation, an example and the rights it can affect, modelled on the privacy considerations of RFC 6973.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational research group document that updates RFC 8280; it recommends no specific practices, only a thought process for analysis.

today: RFC 9620 is an Informational IRTF document that updates RFC 8280 and is not an Internet Standard. Its own text says the methods and guidelines are still being tested for relevance, accuracy and validity.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC gives protocol developers questions to ask when developing or improving protocols, so they can understand how their decisions may influence the exercise of human rights on the Internet. It stresses that the impact of a protocol cannot be deduced from its design alone; its usage and implementation should be studied too.

The questions come from research by the Human Rights Protocol Considerations (HRPC) Research Group of the IRTF. The understanding of human rights rests on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the treaties that follow from it. This document is an iteration of the guidelines in RFC 8280. It is not an IETF product and not a standard, and it does not offer a detailed taxonomy of possible violations.
sections.eli5: It is a list of questions for people who build Internet rules, so they stop and think about how people will be affected.

sections.title: Human Rights Threats
sections.content:
Protocols and standards may harm or enable many rights, among them freedom of expression, freedom of information, non-discrimination, equal protection, participation in cultural life, freedom of assembly and association, privacy and security. Someone denied access to content may be unable to reveal wrongdoing, and a person whose communications are monitored may be dissuaded from associating or taking part in political processes. In the worst case, protocols that leak information can lead to physical danger.

The threat modelling is inspired by RFC 6973 on privacy, which is itself based on security threat analysis. The RFC calls its method a work in progress and not a perfect way to assess human rights risks. It does not try to prioritize some rights over others.
sections.eli5: If a network lets people be watched or blocked, they may be afraid to speak or meet, and sometimes that can put them in real danger.

sections.title: Conducting Human Rights Reviews
sections.content:
Reviews can be done by any participant, such as authors, document shepherds, review team members, advocates or impacted communities. It is easier to influence a technology early; Last Call reviews are still relevant but less likely to cause significant change. The RFC describes five methods, often used together:

  • Analyzing Internet-Drafts with the guidelines model of Section 4.
  • Close reading of a draft for its perceived or speculated impact.
  • Interviews with authors, working group members or experts.
  • Interviews with impacted persons and communities, since rights are best understood from the rights-holder's perspective.
  • Tracing the impacts of implementations, by analyzing running code where it exists.

The RFC calls these methods quite nascent.
sections.eli5: You can check a design by using the checklist, by thinking hard about it, by asking experts, by asking the people affected, or by watching how the finished thing really behaves.

sections.title: The Questionnaire: Network Design Considerations
sections.content:
Section 4 is a questionnaire, useful at any point in design, particularly once a high-level protocol model exists. It does not recommend specific practices, because IETF protocols are too varied. Each consideration has questions, an explanation, an example and a list of rights it can affect.

The first group concerns how the network is built. Intermediaries: does the protocol depend on protocol-specific functions at intermediary nodes? The RFC points to the end-to-end principle and gives encryption of transport information in QUIC as an example of protecting against interference. Connectivity: is it usable on low-bandwidth, high-latency links? Reliability: does it degrade gracefully and resist malicious degradation, noting that attacks on older TLS exploited graceful downgrade? Content signals: does it leak plaintext elements usable for differential treatment? Designers should avoid implicit signals, and explicit signals only where they clearly benefit end users.

Other considerations in this part cover heterogeneity support (many kinds of hardware and applications), adaptability and permissionless innovation, and decentralization, meaning no single point of control.
sections.eli5: These questions ask whether the design works for slow connections, avoids letting middlemen snoop or play favourites, and does not depend on one boss who controls everything.

sections.title: The Questionnaire: Language, Openness and Data
sections.content:
Internationalization asks whether a protocol handles text for humans in many scripts; the RFC says that is normally best done by allowing only Unicode encoded in UTF-8. Localization adapts an implementation for a locale, and internationalization is a precondition for it. Open standards asks whether a protocol is documented well enough to be implemented freely, avoids required proprietary specifications and paywalled normative references, and is free of blocking patents. Accessibility asks whether the design works for people with a range of abilities.

The security-related considerations are integrity, authenticity, confidentiality, security and privacy. They ask, for example, whether data can be altered or forged by an on-path attacker, whether payloads are exposed, whether metadata and traffic analysis are addressed, and whether data minimization is followed. For anonymity, the RFC notes that identifiers are needed for protocols to operate, so true anonymity is very difficult; pseudonymous identifiers and limited scope in time and space (unlinkability) better preserve privacy. It warns that hashing email addresses does not make them non-identifying.
sections.eli5: More questions ask whether everyone can read and use it in their own language, whether anyone can build it, and whether messages are safe from tampering and prying eyes.

sections.title: The Questionnaire: Censorship, Transparency and Remedy
sections.content:
Censorship resistance asks whether the architecture has choke points or exposes identifiers that let traffic be selectively blocked. The RFC lists plaintext DNS queries, the HTTP host header and the TLS Server Name Indication as elements censors can use, and mentions Encrypted ClientHello and DNS over HTTPS as protection. If a protocol enables censorship, designers should aim for error codes that make the reason for blocking clear, as HTTP status code 451 does.

Outcome transparency asks designers to document intended and foreseen effects, since unintended consequences can be architectural, social or economic. Remedy asks whether a protocol can help a harmed party seek remedy without disproportionately harming others' privacy. The RFC concludes that enabling attribution at an individual level is most likely not consistent with human rights. A final miscellaneous item reminds authors that an RFC's publication status signals maturity and affects how widely it is deployed.
sections.eli5: The last questions ask whether the design makes it easy for someone to block things, whether people are told what the design will do, and how to help people who were hurt without spying on everybody.

items.title: Guidelines model
items.text: Review a draft using the questions of Section 4.

items.title: Perceived impact
items.text: Read the draft closely and speculate about effects on networks and society.

items.title: Expert interviews
items.text: Talk to authors, working group members or other experts.

items.title: Impacted communities
items.text: Interview the people who use or are affected by the protocol.

items.title: Tracing implementations
items.text: Analyze running code, in an experiment or on the Internet.
